Baku, October 7, AZERTAC
On October 14-16, the Uzexpocenter Exhibition Complex will host the China Central Asia (Uzbekistan) 2026 Trade Exhibition, according to Uza.uz.
The event will bring together leading manufacturers, exporters, importers, and distributors from both countries. The business platform will focus on showcasing modern goods and services, establishing long-term partnerships, and expanding direct contacts among business community representatives.
Today, China remains Uzbekistan’s leading foreign trade partner. According to the National Statistics Committee, mutual trade turnover reached $11.3 billion in January-July 2026. Meanwhile, imports from China totaled $9.6 billion, and domestic exports to China were recorded at around $1.7 billion.
In 2025, the total investment volume in Uzbekistan reached $43.1 billion, of which $38.2 billion was foreign direct investment. One of the priorities of the ongoing reforms remains not only attracting capital but also establishing high-tech manufacturing enterprises focused on producing high-value-added goods.
Under these conditions, China Central Asia (Uzbekistan) 2026 is an effective, practical tool for turning trade relations into long-term industrial and investment cooperation, helping businesses in both countries develop new joint production projects.

articles.title: Uzbekistan, Russia sign 4 agreements on investment, regional ties - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Uzbekistan, Russia sign 4 agreements on investment, regional ties  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Uzbekistan and Russia signed four agreements on interregional cooperation and investment as representatives of 17 Russian regions, all regions of Uzbekistan and around 400 entrepreneurs gathered for the Third Uzbekistan-Russia Council of Regions in Fergana on Oct. 6.
This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of Uzbekistan.
The meeting brought together regional leaders and business representatives from both countries to discuss expanding direct interregional ties, industrial cooperation, trade, investment and joint projects.
Welcoming remarks from Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Russian President Vladimir Putin were delivered at the meeting by Uzbek Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Khodjaev and Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov.
The broad representation of the two countries provided an opportunity to discuss practical areas of economic cooperation, including the expansion of direct ties between regions and the development of new industrial and investment projects.
"As a practical outcome of the meeting, four agreements were signed. They cover cooperation between the Fergana and Omsk regions, the Surkhandarya Region and Krasnoyarsk Krai, the Namangan Region and the Republic of Dagestan," the statement of the ministry says.
The fourth agreement was an investment deal between Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade and Wildberries for the construction of a Class A logistics complex.
"The practical result was the signing of 4 agreements," the Uzbek Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade said in its statement.
The agreements are expected to provide a framework for expanding cooperation between the participating regions and advancing new investment and business projects.
The meeting also underscored the role of direct regional contacts in developing trade and economic relations between Uzbekistan and Russia, particularly through industrial cooperation, investment and joint ventures.
The next meeting of the Uzbekistan-Russia Council of Regions is scheduled to take place in Omsk, Russia.

articles.title: Oman Trade Corridor Could Link Kazakhstan to Indian Ocean - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Oman Trade Corridor Could Link Kazakhstan to Indian Ocean  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
Kazakhstan could gain a new trade route to the Indian Ocean through Oman’s ports, offering an alternative to its traditional northern and Caspian corridors.
Haitham bin Tariq Al Said, the sultan of Oman, raised the proposal during talks with President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev in Astana on October 6.
He arrived in Astana on October 5, becoming the first Omani sultan to visit Central Asia
“We look forward to developing cooperation in transport and logistics, including the development of a trade corridor through Oman’s ports, as well as strengthening air links between our countries,” the Sultan said.
For landlocked Kazakhstan, Omani ports would provide another potential route to the Indian Ocean. Kazakhstan is already developing the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus, while Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and the United Arab Emirates are studying the CASA railway project through Afghanistan to Pakistani ports. No route, transit countries, cargo volumes, costs, or launch timetable have yet been announced for the Omani proposal.
The talks came immediately after Kazakhstan signed an agreement aimed at settling a long-running dispute over Dunga, an oil field in western Kazakhstan near the Caspian coast. KazMunayGas controls a 60% interest in the project through Dunga Operating GmbH, while Oman Oil Company Limited and Thailand’s PTT Exploration and Production Public Company Limited (PTTEP) each hold 20%.
The dispute concerned costs accumulated under the production-sharing agreement that Kazakhstan considered non-recoverable. On October 5, the Energy Ministry and KazMunayGas signed an agreement to resolve the disputed issues. The agreement will now be sent to the foreign partners, Oman Oil Company Limited and PTTEP, for signature. A new development plan for 2026-2039 provides for production of 67.4 million barrels of oil, as well as capital and operating investment.
Omani capital is also present in Kazakhstan’s gold industry. Maaden International Investment, an Omani state-owned investment fund, held 31.7% of Solidcore’s voting rights as of March 31, 2026, making it the company’s largest shareholder. Solidcore operates gold-mining assets in Kazakhstan.
Kazakhstan and Oman have assembled a portfolio of five major joint projects worth around $3 billion. Two projects totaling approximately $1.1 billion have already been implemented in the energy and railway sectors, while others, including ore-processing projects, are at various stages of development. Oman Investment Authority and Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund Samruk-Kazyna are among the main partners.
During the visit, Samruk-Kazyna and the Oman Investment Authority exchanged an implementation agreement on establishing a joint investment fund and a term sheet for a Rixos hotel project at Blue City in Oman. KazMunayGas and OQ Exploration and Production also agreed to cooperate on investment opportunities in oil and gas exploration and production. The package of agreements covered areas including transport, agriculture, technology, healthcare, mining, and renewable energy.
Despite a joint investment portfolio measured in billions of dollars, merchandise trade between the two countries remains modest. On October 5, the Chamber of International Commerce of Kazakhstan and the Oman Chamber of Commerce and Industry signed a memorandum of understanding. Kazakhstan proposed expanding exports of grain, meat, and organic products, as well as developing joint agricultural processing and logistics projects.

articles.title: Oman and Kazakhstan Advance Indian Ocean Trade Corridor and Settle Dunga Oil Dispute - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Oman and Kazakhstan Advance Indian Ocean Trade Corridor and Settle Dunga Oil Dispute  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Oman and Kazakhstan have committed to developing a multimodal trade corridor connecting Central Asia to the Indian Ocean, anchoring a suite of economic agreements signed during the first-ever visit by an Omani monarch to Astana.
A New Logistics Architecture
Kazakhstan, the world's largest landlocked country, has historically relied on northern transit routes through the Russian Federation. Following the geopolitical shifts of recent years, Astana has aggressively sought alternative pathways to global markets. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said used the latter's historic state visit on Tuesday to formalize plans for a southern exit strategy.
The proposed corridor would leverage Kazakhstan's existing road and rail networks, linking them across the Caspian Sea or through intermediary states to Oman's deep-water ports. Sultan Haitham emphasized that Oman provides direct maritime access to the Gulf, the Indian Ocean, and East Africa, offering a complementary geographic advantage to Kazakhstan's position bridging Europe and Asia.
The initiative dovetails with Kazakhstan's ongoing development of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, known as the Middle Corridor, and its participation in the CASA railway project traversing Afghanistan to Pakistan. While specific cargo volumes, transit tariffs, and physical infrastructure requirements remain undefined, the diplomatic commitment signals a concerted effort to physically integrate Central Asian resource markets with Gulf maritime hubs.
Resolving the Dunga Oil Field Deadlock
The most immediate commercial breakthrough of the summit was the resolution of a protracted dispute over the Dunga oil field, located in Kazakhstan's western Mangystau region. The asset is operated under a production-sharing agreement by Dunga Operating GmbH, which is 60 percent owned by Kazakhstan's state energy firm KazMunayGas, with Oman Oil Company Limited and Thailand's PTTEP each holding a 20 percent stake.
The disagreement centered on capital and operating expenses accumulated during previous phases of extraction, which the Kazakh government had classified as non-recoverable costs under the terms of the consortium's contract. On Monday, the Kazakh Energy Ministry and KazMunayGas signed a settlement agreement resolving these financial discrepancies. The documents will now be transmitted to the Omani and Thai partners for final signature.
The settlement unlocks a new development plan for the Dunga field extending from 2026 to 2039. The operational roadmap projects the extraction of 67.4 million barrels of oil over the 13-year period, supported by renewed capital investment that had been stalled by the cost-recovery dispute. This resolution removes a significant impediment to bilateral investment and demonstrates Astana's willingness to negotiate terms with long-standing Gulf partners.
Historical Foundations and Middle Power Diplomacy
The diplomatic relationship between Oman and Kazakhstan dates back to the immediate aftermath of the Soviet Union's dissolution. Oman was among the first Arab nations to formally recognize Kazakhstan's independence and was an early participant in the consortium established to transport oil from the massive Tengiz field. Despite this early engagement, trade volumes have historically remained modest, reaching approximately 22.9 million Omani rials (roughly $59 million) in the first half of 2026, up from minimal levels in 2025.
The current diplomatic push, spearheaded by Sultan Haitham, represents a deliberate strategy to transition the relationship from political goodwill to structural economic integration. Kazakhstan's foreign policy relies heavily on multi-vector diplomacy, seeking balanced relationships with global superpowers and regional anchors alike. Oman, maintaining its traditional role as a neutral mediator and pragmatic commercial actor in the Middle East, offers Astana an unencumbered gateway to Southern Hemisphere markets.
For the Omani delegation, Kazakhstan presents vast agricultural potential and critical mineral resources that align with Muscat's long-term food security and industrial diversification goals. The establishment of the joint investment fund is explicitly designed to channel Omani sovereign wealth into Kazakh infrastructure, ensuring that the proposed transport corridors have the financial backing necessary to move from concept to physical reality.
Expanding Bilateral Investment
Beyond logistics and hydrocarbons, the two governments executed five formal agreements and ten memoranda of understanding to institutionalize their economic relationship. The summit, which precedes the 35th anniversary of diplomatic ties between the two nations next year, established a joint investment fund and an Oman-Kazakhstan Business Council.
The agreements provide a framework for mutual investment protection and outline cooperation in emerging sectors, including artificial intelligence, digital technologies, and agriculture. Omani capital is already present in Kazakhstan's mining and gold industries, and the new frameworks aim to lower regulatory barriers for sovereign wealth and private sector engagement.
To support the anticipated increase in commercial exchange, the two sides agreed to expand direct air connectivity, a necessary precursor to developing tourism and streamlining executive travel between the two regions.
Strategic Implications
The alignment between Muscat and Astana reflects a broader recalibration of middle powers in the global economy. By securing a reliable partner in the Arab world, Kazakhstan mitigates the logistical vulnerabilities inherent in its geography. For Oman, integrating Kazakh commodities into its port infrastructure reinforces its status as a premier logistics hub outside the congested chokepoints of the upper Persian Gulf. By resolving legacy energy disputes and committing to integrated logistics, the two nations are attempting to engineer a resilient economic axis capable of withstanding regional volatility.

articles.summary: Uzbekistan, Russia sign 2026–2040 science, technology strategy  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Uzbekistan and Russia signed the Protocol of the 27th meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission and a 2026–2040 Strategy for Scientific and Technological Development, setting out a framework for further bilateral cooperation, during a meeting in Fergana on Oct. 6.
This was reflected in the statement by the Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade of Uzbekistan.
The 27th meeting of the Uzbekistan-Russia Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation was co-chaired by Uzbek Deputy Prime Minister Jamshid Khodjaev and Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov.
The sides reviewed the implementation of agreements reached at the highest level and discussed measures to further expand mutual trade and industrial cooperation, according to Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.
It was also noted that the volume of trade increased in January-August 2026.
“Bilateral trade increased by 10% in January-August 2026, exceeding $9 billion,” the ministry said.
Additionally, the sides discussed plans to launch 16 joint enterprises in 2026 in the chemical industry, agriculture and metal processing.
Particular attention was given to the construction of a nuclear power plant in Uzbekistan’s Jizzakh Region. The discussions covered workforce training and the localization of equipment and services as part of the project.
Humanitarian cooperation and tourism were also on the agenda. The sides noted that nearly 1 million Russian tourists visited Uzbekistan in 2025, underscoring the scale of people-to-people ties between the two countries.
The meeting concluded with the signing of the Protocol of the 27th meeting of the Intergovernmental Commission and the Strategy for Scientific and Technological Development of Russia and Uzbekistan for 2026–2040.
The documents are intended to provide a framework for further cooperation in economic, industrial, scientific and technological areas.
The commission meeting was held in Fergana alongside other Uzbekistan-Russia high-level and regional events focused on expanding bilateral economic ties and developing new joint projects.

articles.title: Parsian Exchange transferred millions of dollars for Iran despite sanctions - Iran International
articles.summary: Parsian Exchange transferred millions of dollars for Iran despite sanctions  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Iran’s Bank Parsian, under US sanctions, used its foreign-exchange arm to move millions of dollars abroad through a network of intermediaries, according to an Iran International investigation based on leaked internal correspondence and transaction records.
The documents, covering the period from November 2022 to May 2023, show how Iran’s central bank and other financial institutions used Parsian Exchange, also known as Sarrafi Parsian, to facilitate payments outside Iran.
The transactions involved multiple layers of banks, companies and individuals, according to the records.
Bank Parsian is a private-sector Iranian bank that the US Treasury designated in October 2018, in an action against a network of companies financing the Basij paramilitary force.
The correspondence shows that four years after the designation, Bank Parsian was still arranging international payments through layered channels.
In most cases, no foreign currency actually left Iran. Foreign currency proceeds from oil, petrochemical and other exports were held in accounts overseas. At Bank Parsian’s instruction, Parsian Exchange transferred funds held in those accounts to overseas bank accounts designated by Iranian importers.
But the payments did not appear to come from the Iranian government, sanctioned banks or the Central Bank of Iran (CBI). Instead, they appeared to originate from private companies, with Parsian Exchange acting as an intermediary.
The process
In a typical transaction documented in the files, an Iranian importer—such as carmaker Iran Khodro—sought foreign currency from the CBI to pay a supplier overseas.
The CBI sold the foreign currency to Bank Parsian, according to the documents. The funds were then held at another Iranian bank in an account belonging to a separate individual or company, described in the records as a “trustee”.
The documents showed that Parsian Exchange facilitated the movement of this money between foreign accounts.
Many of the recipient accounts identified in the documents were held at banks in the United Arab Emirates, China and Hong Kong.
The documents show that, by structuring the transactions through these layers, Parsian Exchange obscured the money trail.
Iran International found no evidence that the banks in the UAE and China knowingly facilitated Iran’s efforts to circumvent US sanctions.
Bank Parsian and Parsian Exchange did not respond to Iran International’s requests for comment.
People behind the letters
Parsian Exchange is a subsidiary of Bank Parsian. The bank directly owns 90% of the company, with the remaining roughly 10% held through Parsian Financial Group, its investment arm.
Iran International identified 33 instruction letters in the leaked documents that directed the movement of UAE dirhams, Chinese yuan and US dollars, with a total value of roughly $36 million.
Almost all the letters were signed by Alireza Alaei, Bank Parsian’s head of international affairs. He joined Parsian Exchange’s board as vice chairman in early 2020 and has served as chairman since mid-2020.
Many of the letters were addressed to Rasoul Salehi Oskouei, Parsian Exchange’s chief executive. Official records show he joined the company’s board in early 2018 and has served as vice chairman and chief executive since early 2020.
Salehi Oskouei had also served at another bank-owned exchange company. More than 12 years before joining Parsian Exchange, he sat on the board of Sepehr Exchange, an affiliate of Bank Saderat, from early 2006 to mid-2008
A review of Parsian Exchange’s current and former executives shows a recurring pattern of ties to Bank Parsian and Setad, the economic conglomerate controlled by Iran’s supreme leader.
Alaei joined the company’s board in early 2020 as a representative of Tamin Andish Pars, a Bank Parsian affiliate, and remains on the board. He also served on the board of Parsis Kish starting in 2015, representing Parsian Insurance.
Hesam Shams Alam, who served on Parsian Exchange’s board from 2010 to 2014, had also sat on the board of Bank Parsian. In 2013, he joined the board of Tadbir Investment Group as a representative of Tadbir Industry and Mine Development, an affiliate of Setad.
Instructions for payments
The letters follow a consistent pattern. Alaei sent them to the international departments of other Iranian banks, including Saman, Shahr, Eghtesad Novin, Tourism Bank, Bank Melli and Bank Mellat, all sanctioned by the United States.
The letters were typically sent about 10 days after the banks purchased foreign currency from the Central Bank of Iran. In its letters to the other banks, Bank Parsian said the foreign currency had been “purchased from the central bank” and was being held “in a trustee account” at the recipient bank.
This is where Parsian Exchange came in. Bank Parsian asked the third-party bank to transfer the funds through Parsian Exchange to the ultimate beneficiary.
The subject line of each letter described the funds as being transferred via an intermediary, meaning the payment abroad was made in the name of a private individual or company rather than an Iranian bank or the state.
In a letter dated early 2023, Alaei sent a letter to the international division of the Tourism Bank. He asked the bank to transfer $990,000 held in a trustee account to an account belonging to SEALION General Trading Limited. A review of public records shows the company was active in Hong Kong.
In May 2023, Alaei asked Tourism Bank’s international affairs division to transfer $750,000 to an account held by SAHERI TRADING LIMITED, also registered in Hong Kong.
Bank-owned exchanges
More than 500 licensed exchange companies are currently registered in Iran, 28 of them owned by banks.
By revenue, Parsian Exchange ranks second among them.
Adjusted to September 2026 prices, Melli Exchange, affiliated with Bank Melli, reported annual operating revenue of 1,253 trillion rials. Parsian Exchange ranked second with 1,168 trillion rials, followed by Omid Sepah Exchange, affiliated with Bank Sepah, with 1,129 trillion rials.
Iranian banks began setting up exchange companies more than two decades ago.
Sepehr Exchange, owned by Bank Saderat, was the first exchange company established by an Iranian bank on 25 July 2004. Parsian Exchange followed two weeks later.
Sepah, the state-owned bank with long-standing ties to the armed forces, owns three separate exchange companies. Bank Melli also operates Melli Exchange.
Sanctions
Parsian Exchange has never been named on the US sanctions list. Under US rules, however, a company owned 50 percent or more by a sanctioned entity is automatically covered by the same sanctions, so US persons are already barred from dealing with it.
In April 2026 the U.S. Treasury sanctioned a company it identified as Bank Parsian’s “rahbar”—a private firm that manages the bank’s overseas payments—and in July 2026 an exchange house it said had contracts with the bank.
The United States has targeted bank-owned exchange companies since 2008, when it sanctioned the exchange arm of the Export Development Bank of Iran.
For about a decade, no new sanctions were imposed targeting exchange companies linked to the Islamic Republic until 2018.
By September 2026, the United States had sanctioned a total of 20 exchange companies based in Iran, including six bank-owned exchanges: Export Development Exchange, Dey Exchange, Sina Exchange, and Hekmat Iranian, Ansar and Omid exchanges, all three of which are subsidiaries of Bank Sepah.
More than three years after Joe Biden took office as president, Washington sanctioned five Iranian exchange companies on June 25, 2024: Hekmat Iranian Exchange, affiliated with the former Hekmat Iranian Bank; Omid Exchange, affiliated with Bank Sepah; Sadaf Exchange; Siavash Nourian Exchange; and Atropars Exchange.
It was the largest round of sanctions targeting Iranian exchange houses since Trump left office.
After Trump returned to the presidency, a new wave of sanctions on Iranian exchange houses began in 2025. By September 2026, the United States had sanctioned 11 more exchange houses.

articles.title: Kobakhidze Lauds Growing Economic Ties With China, Talks About Exploring New Markets - Civil Georgia
articles.summary: Kobakhidze Lauds Growing Economic Ties With China, Talks About Exploring New Markets  Civil Georgia
articles.full_text:
Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze lauded Georgia’s expanding economic ties with China at an October 7 government meeting, while stressing the government’s efforts to explore new markets, including through ongoing trade talks with South Korea, Serbia, and the Gulf Cooperation Council.
Speaking of China, Kobakhidze highlighted growing exports and investment, an expanded free trade agreement, and increased direct flights between the two countries.
“Expanding our economic relations with China is very important,” Kobakhidze said, arguing that the expanded free trade agreement was already producing “concrete, tangible results” and citing recent figures from Georgia’s foreign trade and foreign direct investments.
“In January-August, exports of Georgian products to China increased by 177%,” he said, adding “the agreements we conclude in terms of economic cooperation produce concrete results, and this figure is one of the clearest manifestations of that.”
He also said that fourteen flights are operated weekly between Georgia and China after the addition of new direct flights, calling it “of great importance” to Georgia.
According to the GD Prime Minister, Chinese investment in Georgia is also growing. “China ranked first in the first half of this year,” Kobakhidze said, adding that “in terms of foreign direct investment, investment from China amounted to USD 236 million.”
Preliminary data released by the National Statistics Office of Georgia (Geostat) for the second quarter of 2026 showed China overtaking the United Kingdom as Georgia’s largest foreign investor.
Kobakhidze also said the government had been “working very actively” with Central Asian countries and had achieved “serious, tangible results,” while free trade talks are ongoing with other countries and regions, including with South Korea, Serbia, and Gulf countries.
“Negotiations on free trade agreements with the Republic of Korea, Serbia, and the Gulf Cooperation Council are also in an active phase,” he said. According to Kobakhidze, once the process is completed, Georgia will gain access to a market of 120 million people, which he described as “strategically very important” for the country.
- 30/12/2025 – Contesting West, Aligning with Rest: Georgian Dream’s Foreign Policy in 2025 and Beyond
Kobakhidze’s remarks come amid deepening ties between Tbilisi and Beijing. Georgia and China elevated their bilateral relations to a “comprehensive strategic partnership” in June 2026, three years after establishing a strategic partnership in 2023.
In April 2026, the two countries also signed a protocol upgrading their free trade agreement, with the Chinese Embassy saying the changes were intended to further promote and facilitate direct investment between the two countries.
The agreement follows Georgia’s intensified ties with China against the backdrop of its deteriorating relations with traditional Western partners, including the U.S and the EU, and concerns over Chinese influence in Georgia. On June 8, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a bill requiring a report on Russian and Chinese influence and intelligence assets in Georgia, as well as a five-year strategy for U.S.-Georgia relations.

articles.title: Explainer | What’s behind the Turkey–Azerbaijan spat? - OC Media
articles.summary: Explainer | What’s behind the Turkey–Azerbaijan spat?  OC Media
articles.full_text:
A variety of tenuously connected issues have exposed a deeper divide over the unequal power dynamics between Ankara and Baku.
‘One nation, two states’, was how former Azerbaijani President Heydar Aliyev often referred to the inseparable ties between Turkey and Azerbaijan.
In the decades since Azerbaijan’s independence, Turkey has proven to be Baku’s strongest and most consistent ally across a wide spectrum of areas of cooperation. While Turkey has denied directly participating in the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, Turkish defence support for Azerbaijan (along with Israeli arms) were instrumental to the victory over Armenia.
However, in recent days, simmering tensions have bubbled to the surface, centred around disputes about Azerbaijan’s restrictions on religious freedom, Ankara’s distaste of Baku’s alliance with Israel, and questions over Turkish support during the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War. Deeper down, the spat has also highlighted Azerbaijan’s increasingly strident geopolitical posture — and Turkey’s willingness to assert its ‘big brother’ status.
‘A headscarf ban in our brotherly country Azerbaijan’
The latest row appears to have been set off by Azerbaijan’s apparent implementation of a controversial ban on the wearing of hijabs in schools.
Efforts by the Azerbaijani government to restrict hijabs in schools have long been a hot-button issue domestically, with the authorities walking back a ban in 2010 after protests. Though Turkey itself had such a ban until 2014, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has since fashioned himself a champion of the rights of Muslim women to openly practice their religion, including the wearing of hijabs.
In his speech at the UN General Assembly in September, Erdoğan criticised restrictions on wearing hijabs in schools, calling it ‘an attack on women’s most fundamental rights’ and linking the issue to ‘Islamophobia’, which he said is ‘spreading like the plague in the West’. Erdoğan did not mention Azerbaijan by name, but many viewed the comments as being directed at Baku.
Turkish media and politicians linked to the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) have also condemned the decision and urged Erdoğan to raise the issue with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. At the same time, religious organisations in Turkey have held protests outside the Azerbaijani consulate in Istanbul calling for a retraction of the restrictions, with some speakers escalating their rhetoric and calling into question the fundamentals of the ‘brotherly nation’ narrative.
‘The media’s portrayal of this decision as “a headscarf ban in our brotherly country Azerbaijan” does not reflect the truth’, said literary scholar Ahmet Kerim Artuk at the protest.
‘Because of its secular authoritarianism, Islamophobia, and its collaboration with Zionist oppressors in foreign policy, this administration cannot be our brother. The Baku administration has added the tears of our veiled Azerbaijani sisters to the blood of our martyrs in Gaza’, Artuk continued, connecting the hijab ban to Azerbaijan’s longstanding ties with Israel, one of the thorniest issues between Baku and Ankara.
Azerbaijan’s strong ties with Israel
Azerbaijan’s symbiotic relationship with Israel has increasingly become a source of controversy since the beginning of the war in Gaza. While the majority of the Muslim world — including Turkey — has condemned the war and the deaths of tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians caused by Israel’s indiscriminate bombing, Azerbaijan has remained neutral.
For Baku, Israeli arms have been crucial to the modernisation of the Azerbaijani military, and for Israel, Azerbaijani fossil fuels continue to dominate imports to the country. Both countries have also utilised their relationship as a means of demonstrating what they deem their respective religious tolerance.
Nonetheless, the rhetorical links made by Turkish religious figures between the hijab ban and the Azerbaijan–Israel alliance illustrate the issue remains unresolved.
Hülya Şekerci, the founder of the Turkish religious rights organisation Özgür-Der, said at the 3 October protest that, ‘our resistance in Palestine is the same as our struggle for the right to wear a headscarf in Azerbaijan’.
‘We can never call an administration that continues to sit opposite the murderer [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu while he is being protested against and halls are being emptied at the UN General Assembly, and that develops a strategic partnership with Zionist murderers, a brotherly state’, she added.
Şekerci was referring to another recent source of controversy when the Azerbaijani delegate remained in the UN hall to listen to Netanyahu’s speech in September even as dozens of others left the room in protest.
Absent other intermediaries, Azerbaijan has tried to act as a mediator between Israel and Turkey. In 2025, Azerbaijan hosted talks with Turkish and Israeli officials over disputes about Syria.
In August 2026, the Israeli media outlet Ynet reported, citing sources, that Azerbaijan’s efforts to reduce tensions between the two countries were continuing ‘behind the scenes’.
‘Have [Israel] and Turkey lost your minds? You are our friends, and Turkey is our friend too’, an unnamed Azerbaijani official reportedly told Ynet.
‘What are we supposed to do if, God forbid, you start fighting? That is why it is important to reduce the tensions immediately’.
Amidst criticism in Turkey over Azerbaijan’s trade ties with Israel, pro-government Azerbaijani news agency APA published an article seeking to show that trade between Turkey and Israel continues, namely through Turkish-owned vessels carrying cargo to Israeli ports under the flags of other countries. The article was later apparently deleted before being republished the next day.
At the same time, some secular segments of Turkish society tend to view Azerbaijan’s ties with Israel more favourably.
For example, prominent Turkish journalist Yılmaz Özdil has argued that Baku’s diplomatic approach towards Israel has been more effective than Ankara’s. In his remarks, Özdil also emphasised that Azerbaijan relied on Israeli rather than Turkish weapons to regain control over Nagorno-Karabakh.
Azerbaijan’s regional ambitions
This is not the first time that Azerbaijan and Turkey have been at odds over the issue of normalisation with Armenia.
Relations between Azerbaijan and Turkey deteriorated sharply in 2009 during the football diplomacy between Turkey and Armenia, but tensions later subsided.
The Second Nagorno-Karabakh War in 2020 strengthened the strategic partnership between Azerbaijan and Turkey, with Ankara strongly supporting Baku during the conflict. Turkey had already closed its border with Armenia in 1993 in response to the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and maintained that the border would not reopen without progress between Armenia and Azerbaijan.
However, Aliyev has increasingly leaned into a more self-aggrandising view of the war, saying earlier in October that ‘we achieved [the victory] entirely on our own’.
‘Everyone has a powerful backer behind them, so to speak — some even have several. But we stood alone’, Aliyev said.
He doubled-down on the remarks later in his speech, adding, ‘When we needed help, no one helped us’.
It was a striking departure from his own words offered shortly after the conclusion of the war in December 2020, when he said, ‘From the first days of the [war], or rather from the first hours, we have felt the support of Turkey’.
‘[Erdoğan] said that Azerbaijan was not alone and Turkey was always with Azerbaijan’, Aliyev added.
Previously, in 2024, Erdoğan had himself claimed a share in the victory after the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, prompting criticism in the state-run newspaper, Azerbaijan. At the time, Erdoğan said that Turkey could ‘enter Israel just as we entered Karabakh and Libya.’
At the same time, Turkey has otherwise maintained it did not directly participate in the war beyond providing support. Azerbaijan, for its part, has also repeatedly stated no foreign troops directly took part in the hostilities.
Another bone of contention are disagreements over normalisation with Armenia, which Baku has long asserted must be linked to its own peace process with Yerevan.
After Azerbaijan regained control over Nagorno-Karabakh in 2023, the regional situation changed. Turkey began to pursue the normalisation of relations with Armenia more actively, including discussions on reopening the border, restoring transport links and establishing diplomatic relations.
At the same time, while Turkey has long viewed itself as the ‘big brother’ in the bilateral relationship, Azerbaijan appears to be questioning the nature of this dynamic, given its increasingly strident geopolitical stance and its self-declared status as a regional power.
Azerbaijan’s victory in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict and growing energy ties with the EU have bolstered its view of itself as a power-broker in the region, and one that can have its own foreign policy — distinct from Turkey or other stronger countries in the area.
After a Russian anti-air missile mistakenly downed an Azerbaijan Airlines passenger jet in 2024, killing 38 people, Baku reacted strongly, sending its longstanding ties with Moscow into an unprecedented downturn. At the time, Russian commentators appeared to be surprised at the extent and strength of Azerbaijan’s reaction.
Nonetheless, the intensified confrontation has since been resolved, and Azerbaijan appears to be back to its old tricks with Russia, engaging in a mostly behind-the-scenes alliance that rises to the surface occasionally, such as when Baku agreed to release a jailed French national in exchange for the removal of Uzbek-Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov from sanctions in September.
The public theatrics of the spat with Turkey may indicate a similar approach is at work.

articles.title: Tajikistan’s Central Asian trade turnover reaches $1.67 billion in eight months - streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.summary: Tajikistan’s Central Asian trade turnover reaches $1.67 billion in eight months  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
Tajikistan's trade turnover with its Central Asian neighbors reached $1.67 billion during the first eight months of 2026, accounting for approximately 18 percent of the country's total foreign trade, according to official economic data. The figures highlight a sustained effort by Dushanbe to deepen economic integration within the region, reducing historical reliance on external markets and remittance-dependent economic models.
Kazakhstan remains Tajikistan's primary trading partner within the Central Asian bloc, underscoring Astana's position as the region's dominant economic engine and logistical hub. The robust trade volumes between the two nations encompass a wide array of goods, including energy resources, agricultural products, machinery, and construction materials. For Tajikistan, a landlocked, mountainous nation with limited domestic industrial capacity, securing reliable supply chains from its more industrialized neighbors is critical for maintaining domestic price stability and supporting infrastructure development.
Shifting economic dependencies
Historically, Tajikistan's economy has been heavily dependent on remittances from migrant workers, primarily those employed in the Russian Federation, alongside exports of raw materials such as cotton and aluminum. However, the geopolitical and economic disruptions of recent years have accelerated a strategic pivot toward regional self-reliance and intra-Central Asian commerce. The $1.67 billion recorded in trade with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan reflects a deliberate policy shift aimed at diversifying trade routes and fostering regional supply chains that are less vulnerable to external sanctions or global logistical bottlenecks.
Uzbekistan, under its current reform-oriented leadership, has also emerged as a vital partner for Tajikistan. The normalization of relations between Dushanbe and Tashkent over the past decade has led to the reopening of border crossings, the establishment of joint industrial zones, and a significant increase in cross-border trade. Uzbek manufacturing and agricultural exports now play a crucial role in Tajik domestic markets, while Tajik hydroelectric potential and mineral resources offer complementary value to the broader regional economy.
The integration of these economies is further facilitated by ongoing infrastructure projects aimed at improving regional connectivity. Road and rail networks linking the capitals and major industrial centers of Central Asia are being upgraded to reduce transit times and lower the cost of goods. For a country like Tajikistan, where the cost of logistics can severely impact the final price of imported goods, improvements in regional transit corridors are directly tied to inflation control and household purchasing power.
Energy and agricultural synergies
A significant component of the regional trade dynamic involves the exchange of energy and agricultural products. Tajikistan possesses vast hydroelectric resources, primarily generated by the Rogun and Nurek dams, which produce surplus electricity during the summer months. Through the Central Asian power ring, Tajikistan is able to export this surplus to neighboring countries, particularly Afghanistan and Uzbekistan, while importing thermal power and fossil fuels during the winter when domestic demand peaks and hydroelectric output declines.
Agriculture also forms a cornerstone of intra-regional trade. Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are major exporters of wheat, flour, and processed food products, which are essential for Tajikistan's food security. In return, Tajikistan exports early-season fruits, vegetables, and cotton textiles to its neighbors. This complementary agricultural trade helps stabilize food prices across the region and provides a reliable market for Tajik farmers, who have increasingly adopted modern irrigation and greenhouse technologies to extend their growing seasons and improve crop yields.
Primary components of intra-regional trade
- Energy Exchange: Tajik hydroelectric surplus exported in summer; thermal power and fossil fuels imported in winter.
- Agricultural Goods: Wheat and processed foods imported from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan; early-season fruits and cotton exported.
- Industrial Materials: Machinery and construction materials flowing from more industrialized neighbors to support Tajik infrastructure projects.
Challenges to deeper integration
Despite the positive trajectory in trade volumes, significant challenges remain to achieving full economic integration in Central Asia. Border demarcation disputes, particularly in the Ferghana Valley where the borders of Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan intersect, have occasionally led to localized tensions and the temporary closure of transit routes. Resolving these legacy Soviet-era border issues is a prerequisite for the seamless movement of goods and labor across the region.
Furthermore, the shadow of larger external economies, notably China and Russia, continues to influence regional trade dynamics. While intra-Central Asian trade is growing, it still represents a fraction of the total trade volume that these nations conduct with Beijing and Moscow. Chinese investments in infrastructure and mining, and Russian dominance in energy markets and labor migration, mean that Central Asian economies must carefully balance their regional integration efforts with their broader international obligations.
Nevertheless, the $1.67 billion trade milestone achieved in the first eight months of 2026 demonstrates a clear and measurable commitment to regional economic solidarity. As Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan, Turkmenistan, and Tajikistan continue to align their customs regulations, invest in cross-border infrastructure, and promote joint industrial ventures, the Central Asian market is gradually transforming from a collection of fragmented post-Soviet economies into a more cohesive and resilient economic bloc.

Tashkent, Uzbekistan (UzDaily.uz) — Uzbekistan’s Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade Laziz Kudratov held talks with Oman’s Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to Uzbekistan Wafa Jabr Nasir Al-Busaidi on 6 October.
The sides discussed the current state of trade and economic relations and prospects for their further development.
Particular attention was paid to accelerating the implementation of investment projects included in the bilateral portfolio.

Uzbekistan and Oman also intend to continue systematic efforts to expand trade, economic and investment cooperation.

articles.title: Russia Balances Relationship with Iran and Other Gulf States - The Jamestown Foundation
articles.summary: Russia Balances Relationship with Iran and Other Gulf States  The Jamestown Foundation
articles.full_text:
Executive Summary:
- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on April 27 about the ongoing conflict in and around Iran. The visit highlighted the two states’ Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty, signed in January 2025.
- Russia has reaped some economic benefits from Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which raised oil demand and prices and caused the United States to ease sanctions on Russian oil already at sea. If Moscow shows robust military support for Iran, however, it risks damaging economic and diplomatic ties with other Gulf states.
- Russia is constrained from acting as a main mediator in the Iran conflict due to its war against Ukraine. The Iran conflict also endangers key trade corridors, including the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), which links Russia and Iran via the Caucasus.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on April 27 to discuss the ongoing conflict in and around Iran (The Moscow Times; Interfax, April 27). Araghchi’s visit to Moscow highlighted the two states’ Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty—which Putin and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed in January 2025—and raised questions about how Moscow benefits from the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran (President of Russia, April 21, 2025). During the meeting, Putin praised the Iranian people for “fighting for their independence and sovereignty” (President of Russia, April 27). Moscow aims to secure benefits from the Hormuz Strait crisis to gain additional leverage in negotiations on its war against Ukraine.
Russia’s support for Iran could sour its relations with wealthy Gulf monarchies. Russia has sought to benefit from the conflict between the United States, Israel, and Iran that began on February 28, particularly following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz (Anadolu Ajansı, June 5). Iran’s decision to close the strait by planting naval mines, deploying coastal missile batteries, and drone swarms surged global energy prices, causing mid-term disruption of the supply chain (see EDM, March 16). Moscow has viewed Tehran as its main ally in the Middle East for many years, providing military and financial assistance amid long-term international sanctions.
The conflict in Iran disrupted international crude oil trade, triggering fuel shortages in the Asian market. Russia has benefited from this shortage, which has increased demand for its oil and gas. After pressure from Asian countries, the United States opted to ease sanctions on Moscow’s seaborne oil exports as of March 12, allowing purchases of Russian oil that are stranded on tankers at sea (Meduza, March 13). Washington intended the move to mitigate global energy price spikes. Russia was able to take advantage of increased oil demand and eased sanctions by selling down some of the 140 million barrels of oil stranded at sea due to sanctions.
Russia fears that a protracted conflict will jeopardize key projects in Iran. Among them are the Bushehr nuclear power plant, which has been repeatedly struck during the conflict, the Sirik thermal power station, and the ZN Vostok initiatives aimed at developing Iranian oil fields (Vedemosti, March 14, 2018; Russiri.ru, June 10, 2021; Profile.ru, April 9; RBC, April 14). Equally concerning is the disruption of the International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), the principal trade artery linking Moscow and Tehran through the South Caucasus, whose functionality is now at risk. Russia has occasionally attempted to act as a mediator in the Iran conflict, while also seeking to secure economic and political benefits from it (TASS, April 1). Given its partnership with Iran and ongoing war against Ukraine, however, Moscow was not seriously considered as the key intermediary.
Moscow’s war against Ukraine prevents it from mediating other peace processes. Moscow may seek to supply Iran with more weaponry, namely MANPADs and one-way drones, in addition to providing targeting intelligence for Iranian missiles and drones (IST, April 24). Russia’s close ties with Iran’s political establishment, particularly the senior leadership of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), allow the Kremlin to attempt to position itself as a diplomatic channel between the other Gulf states and Tehran amid Iranian strikes on their energy and military infrastructure. On February 28, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov held a call with Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani regarding the U.S.–Israeli Operation Epic Fury (Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Russia, February 2). In the following days, Putin held calls with the leaders of Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Saudi Arabia, and Lavrov spoke with Oman’s foreign minister.
Moscow is no longer positioning itself as a primary mediator in the Iran conflict. On May 18, Lavrov stated that Moscow is “not trying to enter this negotiation process,” adding that it does not try to interfere with the process between the United States and Iran and wishes it success (RT, May 18). Russia remains hesitant to provide robust military support to the Iranian regime as it struggles in its war against Ukraine. Such a restrained posture, especially considering Putin’s failure to meaningfully assist partners in Syria and Venezuela, may further delegitimize Moscow’s promises to its other partners (see EDM, April 6).
Russia recognizes Iran’s value as a partner and hopes to preserve its role within broader geopolitics. Iran’s ideological and political importance to Russia, however, does not outweigh the strategic value of the wealthy Gulf states, given Moscow’s existing infrastructure projects and economic agreements with them. For instance, on May 12, Saudi Arabia and Russia elevated their partnership by introducing a visa-free regime for up to 90 days, a step designed to deepen economic cooperation and expand mutual tourism (Asharq Al-Awsat, May 12). Trade between the UAE and Russia is more than double that between Russia and Iran (Riddle, April 24). The Iran conflict poses challenges for Moscow, disrupting regional trade and energy infrastructure and forcing it to make risky calculations in a changeable regional environment.

articles.title: Beijing Building Massive Bridge In America’s Backyard - The Daily Caller
articles.summary: Beijing Building Massive Bridge In America’s Backyard  The Daily Caller
articles.full_text:
A Chinese construction conglomerate has laid the groundwork for building Latin America’s longest cable-stayed bridge in Brazil by 2031.
The Salvador-Itaparica Bridge will be built via public-private partnership including Chinese Communications Construction and the state-owned China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), per South China Morning Post. The bridge would grant China access to one of Brazil’s most lucrative international trade flashpoints.
It marks the latest development in the Belt and Road Initiative, (BRI), a Chinese strategy that the State Department has described as an attempt from China to “create economic dependencies and to coerce others.” The BRI involves China investing in the infrastructure of developing countries in the Middle East, Central Asia, Latin America, and Africa. (RELATED: Pentagon Cuba Planning Expands As Army Reserve Surveys Troops For Possible Deployment)
“Brazil is a welcoming environment now for the Chinese, politically and economically…a lot of investment is already there, there’s a huge internal market and many other infrastructure projects have already been done,” Latin American Studies Professor Evan Ellis of the United States Army War College’s Strategic Studies Institute told the South China Morning Post. Brazil is a member of the Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa (BRICS) economic coalition. Comprising of 11 member countries and partner nations, BRICS is a coalition aimed at allowing developing economies to trade without using the American dollar or aligning with western interests.
Brazilian President Lula: China can be our partner, bringing technology to us, and so can the United States. I have no restrictions regarding the United States. But Trump has to understand that he takes care of the United States. I take care of Brazil. https://t.co/MkwOhRMoFM
— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 2, 2026
The Chinese Embassy in Washington told the Daily Caller News Foundation that it’s “not familiar with the specifics.”
The Salvador-Itaparica Bridge would be part of a wider 29-mile project, the South China Morning Post reports. Containing the Port of Salvador and several private terminals, All Saints Bay serves as a vital hub for foreign trade in Brazil. It is considered a key trading region for products including petrochemicals, fuel oil, nickel, iron and vanadium.
Latin America is a long-term interest for China. It has invested in both a Peruvian port and a 3,000 mile-long rail line in Brazil that could enable trade routes that circumvent the Panama Canal , the DCNF reported last September.
However, the upcoming October 25th presidential run-off election may complicate Brazil’s relationship with Beijing is Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro wins, the South China Morning Post reported. Bolsonaro aims to veer away from China dependency and partner with the U.S., including giving America access to the country’s rare earth minerals.
The Trump administration has renewed American interest in Latin America. On Jan. 3rd, American Special Forces conducted a high-stakes raid ousting Venezuela’s socialist dictator Nicolas Maduro. Meanwhile, America has begun to intercept oil shipments headed for Cuba, aiming to suffocate the regime in Havana.

articles.title: Opinion: The 2026 CAMCA Regional Forum Concludes – What’s Next? - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Opinion: The 2026 CAMCA Regional Forum Concludes – What’s Next?  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
The 2026 CAMCA Regional Forum has concluded in Baku after two full days of conversation on a range of topics shaping the future of the region. The closing ceremony included an official announcement that next year’s Forum will take place in Uzbekistan in June of 2027. The question now is: in the lead-up to next year’s convening, how do we build on the connections, ideas and momentum built in Baku to truly advance regional cooperation in the months ahead? How do we turn conversation into action?
The mechanism and catalyst for this will be the CAMCA Network – the dynamic collection of more than 300 talented leaders spread throughout the entire region and beyond – united by a common conviction that a successful future of the CAMCA region lies in intraregional cooperation and collaboration.
Through existing initiatives, such as CAMCA Talking magazine, and forthcoming projects – CAMCA TV and the CAMCA Conversations podcast – the network will utilize these innovative platforms to raise awareness around the important developments taking place within the CAMCA region, and, most importantly, to highlight where regional cooperation is well underway, where more is needed, and how leaders across sectors can do their part to drive tangible collaboration to the next level.
While the CAMCA Network can serve as an important stimulus of this effort, it is critical that we continue to expand the CAMCA community across all sectors and build partnerships with individuals, organizations and companies that share our vision for CAMCA’s connected, collaborative and prosperous future. This is the charge we take from Baku and will be an integral part of CAMCA’s next chapter.
From his time in public service and at the outset of the Rumsfeld Foundation’s work with rising leaders from the region, Secretary Rumsfeld believed in the incredible potential of the CAMCA region, predicated on the ten countries themselves recognizing the benefit of their enhanced cooperation. 20 years ago, there were few who shared his vision or his optimism.
Today, on the heels of the 12th annual CAMCA Forum, this vision has come to life, and global interest and momentum are in CAMCA’s favor. As we look towards the 2027 CAMCA convening in Uzbekistan, we are eager to invite partners from within the region and across the globe to join us in building CAMCA’s next chapter. The groundwork has been laid, and a dedicated and energetic network of regional trailblazers now exists – let’s put it to work and bring CAMCA to a new level.
The CAMCA Regional Forum is an annual, non-partisan event dedicated to promoting dialogue, cooperation, and sustainable economic growth across Central Asia, Mongolia, the Caucasus, and Afghanistan. Established as a premier platform for high-level engagement, the Forum convenes diverse stakeholders from government, business, academia, civil society, and beyond. The Forum is co-organized by the Rumsfeld Foundation, Central Asia-Caucasus Institute, and the CAMCA Network. Learn more at www.camcaforum.org.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the official policy or position of the publication, its affiliates, or any other organizations mentioned.

articles.title: Central Asia Looks to a Possible Trump Visit - The Times Of Central Asia
articles.summary: Central Asia Looks to a Possible Trump Visit  The Times Of Central Asia
articles.full_text:
U.S. President Donald Trump has expressed an interest in visiting Uzbekistan, according to one of his special envoys, raising the possibility that Central Asia could eventually receive its first visit by a sitting American president.
Paolo Zampolli, Trump’s Special Envoy for Global Partnerships and long-time Trump associate, made the comment in an interview with Uzbekistan 24 while visiting the country. “I know that he wants to come to Uzbekistan,” Zampolli said, adding that Trump had personally told him he wanted to make the trip. Zampolli said he was encouraging the idea, but gave no timetable, and there has been no announcement that a visit is being scheduled.
Trump had already publicly indicated that he may visit Kazakhstan. Asked during the November 2025 C5+1 summit if he might become the first U.S. president to visit the country, Trump replied, “I think it’s very possible that we’ll do that.”
The comments come as U.S. engagement with Central Asia is accelerating. Trump hosted all five Central Asian presidents at the White House in November 2025. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has invited him to Kazakhstan, while Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has also invited him to Uzbekistan. Meanwhile, Secretary of State Marco Rubio is reported to be planning a mid-October visit to Samarkand for a C5+1 ministerial, with a delegation expected to include representatives of more than 100 U.S. companies.
Sergio Gor, Trump’s Special Envoy for South and Central Asia, has also been involved in Washington’s engagement across the region. In Uzbekistan, he co-chairs the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council with Saida Mirziyoyeva, head of the presidential administration.
Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan bring different economic and strategic profiles to Washington’s expanding engagement with Central Asia.
Why Kazakhstan Matters
Kazakhstan is Central Asia’s largest economy. Its GDP reached about $306 billion in 2025, accounting for more than half of the combined economy of the five Central Asian states. Its share of accumulated foreign investment is even larger, with Kazakhstan holding roughly two-thirds of the region’s inward FDI stock, according to The Times of Central Asia’s Central Asia Balance Sheet.
Its strategic importance extends beyond those measures. Kazakhstan produces close to 40% of the world’s uranium and is a major oil producer and exporter, supplying primarily European markets. It also holds substantial critical mineral resources and occupies a central position on the Middle Corridor connecting China and Europe.
Recent U.S.-Kazakh commercial agreements include several large transactions. Wabtec has a $4.2 billion locomotive agreement, while Tau-Ken Samruk and Cove Capital have signed transaction documents for at least $1.1 billion in tungsten development. Other agreements cover agricultural machinery, air-traffic management, and additional Boeing aircraft.
Kazakhstan also has a distinct diplomatic role in Trump’s engagement with the Muslim world. In November 2025, Kazakhstan joined the Abraham Accords, becoming the first Central Asian and first non-Arab Muslim-majority country to join the framework.
Why Uzbekistan Matters
With about 39 million people, Uzbekistan is the most populous country in Central Asia. It is also the only state that borders all four of the other Central Asian republics, as well as Afghanistan, giving it a uniquely central geographic position.
Uzbekistan’s economic relationship with Washington is also expanding. Cooperation and projects announced since 2025 span critical minerals, artificial intelligence, agriculture and industrial projects, with projects at different stages of development. Uzbekistan Airways has ordered 22 Boeing 787-9s in a package valued by the U.S. government at about $8.5 billion, with deliveries to take place over several years.
There is also a powerful Islamic historical dimension. Samarkand and Bukhara were among the great cities of the Muslim world, flourishing when Muslim empires were among the world’s leading centers of scholarship, commerce, and political and military power. Bukhara became one of Islam’s great centers of religious learning, while both cities formed part of a wider Persianate Islamic civilization stretching into Iran and across Central Asia.
Samarkand later became the capital of Timur’s empire and one of the Islamic world’s great architectural and cultural centers, while Tashkent is home to the Khast Imam complex and the celebrated Uthman Quran. A presidential visit involving any of these cities could therefore carry symbolism well beyond Central Asia, reflecting engagement with the wider Islamic world and its civilizational heritage.
Which Country Could Host the First Visit?
Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan offer a U.S. president different points of engagement with Central Asia. Kazakhstan brings the region’s largest economy, major energy and mineral resources, substantial accumulated U.S. investment, and an expanding role in transport and digital connectivity. Uzbekistan combines the region’s largest population, a central geographic position, and historic centers of Islamic civilization. Both are deepening their political and commercial ties with Washington.
Zampolli’s comments establish only that Trump has expressed a desire to visit Uzbekistan, not that a trip is being planned or when one might occur. Separately, Trump has said that a visit to Kazakhstan is “very possible,” and Tokayev has invited him. There is currently no announced presidential itinerary for either country, and nothing establishing that the two prospective visits are linked. Either could ultimately become the first visit by a sitting U.S. president to Central Asia.

articles.title: Strategic cooperation with Russia remains key foreign policy priority - Turkmen president - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Strategic cooperation with Russia remains key foreign policy priority - Turkmen president  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. Developing strategic cooperation with Russia remains one of the main directions of Turkmenistan’s foreign policy, President Serdar Berdimuhamedov said today during a phone conversation with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
This was reflected in a press release issued by the press service of the Turkmen government.
The two presidents discussed the development of bilateral relations and the importance of continued interstate dialogue.
“During the telephone conversation, it was noted that the development of strategic cooperation with the Russian Federation remains one of the main priorities of Turkmenistan’s foreign policy,” the report says.
Putin said Russian-Turkmen relations are based on the principles of equality, mutual respect and good-neighborly relations.
He also highlighted Berdimuhamedov’s contribution to strengthening interstate dialogue between the two countries, according to the press service.
Berdimuhamedov expressed gratitude to Putin for his personal attention to and support for the development of Turkmen-Russian relations.
The presidents noted that traditionally friendly relations between Turkmenistan and Russia are based on longstanding ties, trust and mutual understanding.
Putin also conveyed greetings and best wishes to the Chairman of the country’s Halk Maslahaty, Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedov.
Meanwhile, Russia and Turkmenistan maintain a strategic partnership covering trade, energy, transport, diplomacy and humanitarian ties. Russia remains one of Turkmenistan’s key trading partners, with bilateral trade exceeding $1.6 billion annually, according to Turkmen government data.
In 2025, bilateral trade continued to expand, with trade turnover rising 21.4% in the first quarter, while the two sides worked on an intergovernmental action plan for 2025-2027. Cooperation also extends to the fuel and energy sector, industry, agriculture, banking and finance, and digital technologies.
Energy remains an important component of the relationship, although Russia is no longer the main destination for Turkmenistan’s natural gas exports. The two countries have also been developing transport cooperation, including routes linking Turkmenistan with Russia and other markets through the Caspian Sea. Discussions have included the Volga-Caspian Canal with an outlet to the port of Turkmenbashi and the eastern bypass of the Caspian Sea within the International North-South Transport Corridor.
At the political level, Moscow and Ashgabat cooperate through the UN, CIS, the Caspian littoral states and the Central Asia-Russia format. In September 2026, Turkmenistan said preparations were underway for the 14th meeting of the bilateral intergovernmental commission, with the agenda covering trade, energy, transport, finance, industry and other areas.

articles.title: Russia’s Ambition and Its Limits: Where Negotiation Can Begin - SLDinfo.com
articles.summary: Russia’s Ambition and Its Limits: Where Negotiation Can Begin  SLDinfo.com
articles.full_text:
By Pasquale Preziosa
Understanding what future Russia desires requires a preliminary distinction between the country, its ruling class, and the political system that governs it: three closely linked realities whose interests and perspectives do not always coincide. The Kremlin’s decisions bind the Russian state, but they do not necessarily express all the aspirations of its society, nor do they allow us to consider the country’s future behavior as already determined. This distinction also applies to democracies: what changes is the ability of citizens to influence the decisions of those in power, challenge them, and determine their correctness. The central issue, therefore, concerns the strategic project pursued by the Russian leadership and the conditions that may favor, contain, or modify it.
The imperial tradition is a component of Russian political culture and helps explain the difficulty Moscow has in accepting the full autonomy of the states that have emerged in the territory once subject to its rule. On a different level—that of internal separatism—the wars in Chechnya also demonstrate how heavily the maintenance of territorial control weighed on the decision-making of the Russian leadership. Historical interpretations are constructed in hindsight and allow us to recognize a continuity that, as events unfolded, was not always evident.
In the Russian case, the imperial legacy is intertwined with the experience of invasions suffered, from the Napoleonic invasion of 1812 to the Nazi invasion of 1941 against the Soviet Union. The memory of vulnerability and the aspiration to expand its influence thus help explain a strategic culture in which defensive needs and ambitions for power can overlap. Events, however, unfold at different times and under different conditions, and even seemingly similar behaviors may stem from distinct motivations.
Interpreting the present, therefore, requires considering both the weight of historical legacies and the choices that take shape in the face of new circumstances. Imperial continuity represents, in this sense, an important key to understanding Russian politics; its explanatory power must, however, be weighed against changes in the context and the decisions of its protagonists.
Therefore, attributing to Russia an unchanging expansionist nature risks steering the analysis toward a predetermined conclusion, just as it would be simplistic to interpret each of its initiatives as a mere defensive reaction. It is necessary to evaluate statements, actions, capabilities, and constraints as a whole, bearing in mind that intentions may solidify or change in response to the evolving context, the results obtained, and the costs incurred.
The introductory pages of Sabino Cassese’s How to Measure a Democracy help us understand precisely the context in which these intentions take shape and may evolve. Cassese describes the resurgence of nation-states, the deepening of power inequalities, and the weakening of multilateralism in favor of bilateral relations. He also highlights a European contradiction: a persistent capacity to attract, accompanied by a political weakness that exposes the continent to decisions made by others.
His reflection thus offers a framework for interpreting Russian ambitions as well, even without addressing them directly in the pages mentioned here. Equality among states has never eliminated geopolitical hierarchies. In the contemporary world, however, the gap between formal equality and the actual ability to influence international decisions takes on particular significance.
The Kremlin’s project can also be interpreted as an attempt to permanently position Russia among the powers capable of contributing to the definition of rules, freeing it from having to accept those established elsewhere. An explicit reference to this aspiration is found in the March 2023 Foreign Policy Concept, in which Russia presents itself as a “country-civilization” and a major Eurasian and Euro-Pacific power, claiming an autonomous role in the construction of a multipolar order. This self-representation expresses both a conception of Russian identity and the international status that its leadership seeks to guarantee; it documents the way in which power legitimizes itself, without, in and of itself, demonstrating the correspondence between declared principles and actual behavior.
From this approach emerges, first and foremost, the demand for recognition of its own geopolitical status.
Moscow wants to be regarded as an indispensable partner on key strategic issues. Its nuclear arsenal, permanent seat on the Security Council, and ability to influence regional balances underpin this aspiration. Territory is important, but so is the ability to prevent others from making decisions without involving it. For a great power, the ability to obstruct the choices of others can compensate, at least in part, for a lesser capacity for political appeal. Ukraine embodies this interconnection between territory, security, and recognition. In June 2024, Putin made a ceasefire and the start of negotiations contingent on Ukraine’s withdrawal from the entire territory of the four regions claimed by Moscow and its renunciation of NATO membership, demands that went beyond the positions then under Russian military control.
This statement documents the publicly declared objectives at that stage, but, on its own, does not allow us to determine what conditions Moscow might accept in a future agreement. The strategic significance, however, is clear: Moscow sought to dictate both Ukraine’s borders and its international orientation. This reveals a hierarchical conception of relations between states, one that the current Russian leadership expresses toward Ukraine: formal independence can coexist with limited sovereignty in practice, when a neighboring power seeks to determine Ukraine’s alliances and defense capabilities. The Russian proposals of December 2021 confirm that the dispute went beyond Ukraine alone: the demand to block further NATO enlargement and to limit military mobilizations, using the situation in 1997 as a reference point, affected the overall structure of European security.
Interpreting these proposals as evidence of a predefined plan to conquer the entire continent would be arbitrary, but interpreting them as a demand limited to the Donbass would be equally reductive: in fact, they also concerned the distribution of power in Europe.
Here lies a contradiction in the multipolarity proposed by the Kremlin: claiming autonomy from the other great powers while, at the same time, restricting the autonomy of its neighbors. An order with multiple centers of power may, in fact, result in more balanced relations among the great powers and be more coercive toward smaller states. The plurality of poles, in and of itself, does not guarantee freedom for those who live among them.
The relationship between security and control of the geopolitical space must also be examined more closely. Russian perceptions of vulnerability must be included in the analysis, along with Western decisions and their effects. A perception of threat, however, does not make recourse to war inevitable. When a state’s protection depends on the weakness and subordination of neighboring states, the pursuit of security takes on the characteristics of a hegemonic claim. Ukrainian, Polish, and Baltic concerns are therefore part of the same equation and must be considered an integral part of any assessment of European security.
There is, moreover, an internal dimension that is equally important. It is reasonable to interpret the confrontation with the outside world as a means of legitimizing power: the promise of restoring Russia’s greatness can justify demands for discipline and sacrifice. This interpretation remains, however, a hypothesis to be verified, and does not fully explain the Kremlin’s choices. The regime’s continuity, international prestige, and the country’s long-term interests do not necessarily align; a choice that serves to preserve power may, on the contrary, entail lasting costs for society. Asking what Moscow desires therefore also requires asking what costs it is willing to accept and which it can actually bear.
A country’s level of ambition must take into account available economic and financial resources, demographic dynamics, access to technology, military capabilities, and the quality of its foreign relations. Potential international sanctions also affect this balance, increasing costs and limiting the possibilities for pursuing stated objectives.
The relationship with China introduces a further dilemma: the quest for greater autonomy from the West may increase dependence on an economically stronger partner, thereby restricting precisely those same margins of choice that Moscow seeks to expand. Russia aspires to be an autonomous power, but the possibility of realizing this ambition must be assessed in light of the asymmetries and interdependencies that also characterize its relations with Beijing. The future therefore remains open, shaped by the interplay of ambitions, resources, and constraints.
If coercion yields benefits at costs deemed acceptable, the Russian leadership may be encouraged to resort to it again; if, on the other hand, it encounters sustained resistance and a credible prospect for negotiation, it may recalibrate its objectives and instruments. It could also choose to prolong the conflict if it deemed a compromise riskier than continuing it.
None of these outcomes follows automatically from history: each also depends on the assessments of Russian leadership and the choices of other actors. For Europe, these considerations have significant strategic implications: it must have the capacity to protect itself and support Ukrainian autonomy, while at the same time developing a political strategy capable of influencing the costs and benefits that Moscow associates with its choices.
