articles.full_text:
New Delhi presents a strategic ceasefire framework for Eastern Europe
India has officially outlined a specific three-part ceasefire strategy to stop hostilities between Moscow and Kyiv. Foreign Minister S Jaishankar delivered this proposal directly to Ukrainian officials during his recent visit to Eastern Europe. The framework prioritizes stopping direct strikes on energy facilities, ensuring safe passage for commercial ships, and maintaining uninterrupted grain shipments through Black Sea ports.
International diplomatic efforts
Diplomatic sources confirm that Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha recognized this initiative as the most detailed among current international efforts. Other nations, including Egypt, Turkey, and the United States, have also submitted separate negotiation options. Egypt and Turkey primarily target agricultural exports, while American negotiators concentrate on halting power grid attacks. New Delhi combined these critical elements into one unified document to address multiple humanitarian concerns simultaneously.
Changing role in global mediation
Russian President Vladimir Putin recently praised Prime Minister Narendra Modi for offering practical ideas to reach a mutually acceptable resolution. Putin specifically highlighted India's neutral diplomatic position throughout the five-year conflict.
Global observers note that this geopolitical crisis has severely disrupted global supply chains since early 2022. By presenting a concrete framework, Indian diplomats are shifting from simple advocacy to active negotiation. Jaishankar reinforced this evolving position during the Munich Security Conference in Delhi, confirming ongoing practical discussions with both sides. Both warring nations continue evaluating the exact terms. Ukrainian leaders remain open to different negotiation formats. However, they insist any final agreement must protect their critical port infrastructure alongside pausing direct frontline combat operations. New Delhi will likely maintain regular contact with both capitals to refine the proposed steps over the coming weeks.

articles.title: US President plans to visit Uzbekistan, US envoy says - Азия-Плюс
articles.summary: US President plans to visit Uzbekistan, US envoy says  Азия-Плюс
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump intends to visit Uzbekistan, although no date has been set, according to US Special Envoy for Global Partnerships Paolo Zampolli.
Zampolli made the remarks during a recent visit to Tashkent, telling an Uzbek television interviewer that Uzbekistan is on Trump’s “to-do” list, Eurasianet reported.
“I know that he wants to come to Uzbekistan. The President’s schedule is extremely busy. But he told me that he wants to visit Uzbekistan. I also always push this issue,” Uzbek media outlets quoted Zampolli as saying on October 5. “We hope that this visit will take place as soon as possible.”
Zampolli reportedly also described the relationship between Trump and Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev as “unique,” saying the two leaders have developed a friendly and trusting relationship and speak regularly by telephone.
Mirziyoyev has invited Trump to visit Uzbekistan on several occasions. The Trump administration has stepped up engagement with Central Asia over the past 18 months, including efforts to expand US access to the region’s critical mineral resources. Kazakhstan has also sought to host the US president.
US trade delegation to visit Uzbekistan
Washington is expected to further strengthen its engagement with Central Asia this month. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is planning to attend a mid-October meeting of Central Asian foreign ministers in Samarkand under the C5+1 format.
Rubio is expected to be accompanied by a US trade delegation of around 100 representatives. The meeting is aimed at strengthening US trade ties with Central Asia by promoting cooperation on shared regional priorities, according to Sergio Gor, the US special envoy for South and Central Asia.
The trade delegation is expected to explore potential deals across a range of sectors.
During his recent visit to Uzbekistan, Zampolli also expressed US support for the country’s efforts to develop into a regional air transport hub.
Tashkent airport handled 5.4 million passengers in the first six months of 2026, a 17% increase from the same period last year, according to local reports. Airports in Samarkand, Bukhara and Termez have also recorded strong passenger growth.
A recent Boeing forecast reportedly identified Central Asia as a major growth market for aviation over the next two decades. Most new aircraft purchases are expected to serve regional routes, although Central Asian countries are also seeking to expand long-haul capacity.
Uzbekistan committed in 2025 to purchasing 22 Boeing 777 Dreamliners, while Kazakhstan’s Air Astana has also purchased Dreamliners.
“Central Asia should gain importance as governments invest in hubs and national carriers,” the Boeing forecast said, adding that Eurasian airlines would need to expand their combined in-service fleet from more than 6,800 aircraft to 10,820 by 2045 to meet growing travel demand.
Zampolli also said investments by US agricultural and food giant Cargill in Uzbekistan could reach $6 billion. Previous reports had estimated the potential value of Cargill’s investments at between $3 billion and $5 billion, Eurasianet reported.
